steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
## Motivation

Dialogue systems are getting a lot of attention and demand, both in industry and in everyday life, because they have a diverse range of functionalities for user needs. They can be broadly divided into two categories: task-oriented dialogue systems (TOD) and open-domain dialogue systems (ODD). TOD systems are designed for particular problems in a specific domain, and their goal is to perform tasks like ticket or table reservations. So their main focus is completing the task. ODD systems on the other hand have unrestricted conversations about a wide range of topics. So the main challenge for ODD systems is handling consistency and transitioning seamlessly between turns in the conversation.

Like other natural language processing (NLP) tasks, progress in dialogue systems relies heavily on large neural models, and so how effective they are depends on having substantial amounts of training data. This dependence on large scale training data is a challenge for developing dialogue agents, especially in low resource settings where there is limited or no training data. Crowd-sourcing is the main method for creating datasets for dialogue systems, but it is labor intensive and so it has limitations in time, cost, and scalability. Data is scarce for diverse and specific domains, and it is also hard to adapt existing datasets or create completely new ones, so alternative methods for training dialogue systems are needed.

Several methods have been proposed for the data shortage problem in dialogue systems, including semi-supervised learning and data augmentation (DA). Semi-supervised learning is promising, but relying only on existing dialogue datasets is a classic chicken-and-egg problem. DA instead generates conversation samples from external resources, for example unstructured text files and structured data like knowledge graphs. This approach does several things: it diversifies datasets, it introduces novel conversational scenarios, and it gives more control over the flow of the generated conversation.

In this tutorial we want to give a comprehensive overview of methods for conversation augmentation and generation for TOD and ODD systems. We go into the specific challenges that have to be addressed when creating new dialogue data. We also present an overview of evaluation methods and of available datasets that can be used to assess the quality and performance of the generated dialogue data, so that the package for dialogue data creation is comprehensive. By covering these aspects the tutorial gives a holistic understanding of the methods, challenges, and evaluation procedures of dialogue data creation.

- Previous tutorials

  - Conversational Recommender Systems, RecSys 2020: foundations, algorithms; search engines, e-commerce, social networks
  - Conversational Information Seeking: Theory and Application, SIGIR 2022: intro to CIS, advanced topics, state-of-the-art
  - Self-Supervised Learning for Recommendation, CIKM 2022: systematic review of SSL-based recommender systems
  - Limited Data Learning, ACL 2022: methods reducing need for labeled data in NLP, incl. DA and semi-supervised learning
  - Proactive Conversational Agents, WSDM 2023: agents interacting proactively with end users

## Motivation

Dialogue systems are getting a lot of attention and demand, both in industry and in everyday life, because they have a diverse range of functionalities for user needs. They can be broadly divided into two categories: task-oriented dialogue systems (TOD) and open-domain dialogue systems (ODD). TOD systems are designed for particular problems in a specific domain, and their goal is to perform tasks like ticket or table reservations. So their main focus is completing the task. ODD systems on the other hand have unrestricted conversations about a wide range of topics. So the main challenge for ODD systems is handling consistency and transitioning seamlessly between turns in the conversation.

Like other natural language processing (NLP) tasks, progress in dialogue systems relies heavily on large neural models, and so how effective they are depends on having substantial amounts of training data. This dependence on large scale training data is a challenge for developing dialogue agents, especially in low resource settings where there is limited or no training data. Crowd-sourcing is the main method for creating datasets for dialogue systems, but it is labor intensive and so it has limitations in time, cost, and scalability. Data is scarce for diverse and specific domains, and it is also hard to adapt existing datasets or create completely new ones, so alternative methods for training dialogue systems are needed.

Several methods have been proposed for the data shortage problem in dialogue systems, including semi-supervised learning and data augmentation (DA). Semi-supervised learning is promising, but relying only on existing dialogue datasets is a classic chicken-and-egg problem. DA instead generates conversation samples from external resources, for example unstructured text files and structured data like knowledge graphs. This approach does several things: it diversifies datasets, it introduces novel conversational scenarios, and it gives more control over the flow of the generated conversation.

In this tutorial we want to give a comprehensive overview of methods for conversation augmentation and generation for TOD and ODD systems. We go into the specific challenges that have to be addressed when creating new dialogue data. We also present an overview of evaluation methods and of available datasets that can be used to assess the quality and performance of the generated dialogue data, so that the package for dialogue data creation is comprehensive. By covering these aspects the tutorial gives a holistic understanding of the methods, challenges, and evaluation procedures of dialogue data creation.

## Previous tutorials

Our tutorial builds on two key concepts, conversational systems and DA. Recent tutorials that discuss these concepts are:

- Conversational Recommender Systems in RecSys 2020. This tutorial is about the foundations and algorithms for conversational recommendation and how they are applied in real-world systems like search engines, e-commerce, and social networks.

- Conversational Information Seeking: Theory and Application in SIGIR 2022. This tutorial gives an introduction to Conversational Information Seeking (CIS) and covers recent advanced topics and state-of-the-art approaches.

- Self-Supervised Learning for Recommendation in CIKM 2022. This tutorial presents a systematic review of state-of-the-art recommender systems based on self-supervised learning (SSL).

- Limited Data Learning in ACL 2022. This tutorial gives an overview of methods that reduce the need for labeled data in NLP, including DA and semi-supervised learning.

- Proactive Conversational Agents in WSDM 2023. This tutorial introduces methods that give conversational agents the ability to interact proactively with end users.

The previous tutorials focus either on conversational systems or on the data scarcity problem, but this tutorial explores in depth the challenges of augmenting and creating conversational data, and highlights the unique difficulties of the conversational context. As far as we know, no tutorial has focused specifically on techniques for creating datasets for dialogue systems.

## Target audience and prerequisites

This tutorial is for professionals, students, and researchers in information retrieval and natural language processing who are interested in conversational AI. Familiarity with machine learning, deep learning, and transformers is required. No prior knowledge of dialogue system models or of data augmentation methods is needed.

## Tutorial material

The tutorial slides, a collection of essential references, and other support materials are on the tutorial website https://dataug-convai.github.io.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
## Motivation

The development of dialogue systems has received significant attention and demand in both industry and everyday life, thanks to the diverse range of functionalities they offer to meet user needs. These systems can be broadly classified into two categories: task-oriented dialogue systems (TOD) and open-domain dialogue systems (ODD) [1]. TOD systems are designed to address particular problems within a specific domain, with the objective of performing tasks like ticket or table reservations. Their primary focus is thus task completion. ODD systems, on the other hand, engage in unrestricted conversations on a wide range of topics [1]. The main challenge of ODD systems therefore lies in handling consistency and seamless transitions between turns in the conversation.

As in other natural language processing (NLP) tasks, the progress of dialogue systems relies heavily on large neural models, and as a result their effectiveness depends on the availability of substantial amounts of training data [2]. This dependence on large scale training data challenges the development of dialogue agents, particularly in low resource settings with limited or no training data. While crowd-sourcing is the primary method for generating datasets for dialogue systems, its labor intensive nature brings limitations in time, cost, and scalability [3]. The scarcity of data for diverse and specific domains, together with the difficulty of adapting existing datasets or generating entirely new ones, calls for alternative methods of training dialogue systems.

To tackle the data shortage in dialogue systems, several methods have been proposed, including semi-supervised learning and data augmentation (DA) [4]. While semi-supervised learning is a promising approach, relying solely on existing dialogue datasets presents a classic chicken-and-egg problem. DA, on the other hand, generates conversation samples from external resources, such as unstructured text files and structured data like knowledge graphs. This approach serves multiple purposes: it diversifies datasets, introduces novel conversational scenarios, and gives more control over the flow of the generated conversation.

In this tutorial, we aim to offer a comprehensive overview of conversation augmentation and generation methods for TOD and ODD systems. We delve into the specific challenges that must be addressed when creating new dialogue data. To provide a comprehensive package for dialogue data creation, we also present an overview of evaluation methods and available datasets that can be used to assess the quality and performance of the generated dialogue data. By covering these aspects, our tutorial offers a holistic understanding of the methods, challenges, and evaluation procedures involved in dialogue data creation.

## Previous tutorials.

Our tutorial builds upon two key concepts: conversational systems and DA. Recent tutorials that discuss these concepts include:

- • Conversational Recommender Systems [5] in RecSys 2020. This tutorial focuses on the foundations and algorithms for conversational recommendation and their application in real-world systems like search engines, e-commerce, and social networks.

- • Conversational Information Seeking: Theory and Application [6] in SIGIR 2022. The tutorial provides an introduction to Conversational Information Seeking (CIS), covering recent advanced topics and state-of-the-art approaches.

- • Self-Supervised Learning for Recommendation [7] in CIKM 2022. This tutorial presents a systematic review of state-of-the-art self-supervised learning (SSL)-based recommender systems.

- • Limited Data Learning [4] in ACL 2022. This tutorial offers an overview of methods that alleviate the need for labeled data in NLP, including DA and semi-supervised learning.

- • Proactive Conversational Agents [8] in WSDM 2023. This tutorial introduces methods for equipping conversational agents with the ability to interact proactively with end users.

Unlike previous tutorials that focus on either conversational systems or the data scarcity problem, this tutorial provides an in-depth exploration of the challenges of augmenting and creating conversational data, highlighting the unique difficulties of the conversational context. To the best of our knowledge, no tutorial has specifically focused on dataset creation techniques for dialogue systems.

## Target audience and prerequisites.

This tutorial is designed for professionals, students, and researchers in information retrieval and natural language processing who are specifically interested in conversational AI. Familiarity with machine learning, deep learning, and transformers is required. No prior knowledge of dialogue system models or data augmentation methods is necessary.

## Tutorial material

Tutorial slides, a collection of essential references, and other support materials are available at the tutorial website https://dataug-convai.github.io.
